1:
Weariness of life is the opening note, and Gill measures how strange it is. No temporal blessing is more desirable than life, and soul and body are companions loath to part. Yet this man loathed his and longed to be rid of it, and Gill rules out the usual causes: not guilt pressing him until he could not bear to live, as with Cain and Judas, nor indwelling sin, nor grief at the sins of others. Clarke draws a doctrine from the word for soul, which cannot mean animal life, being distinguished in the Hebrew from a term that does, and takes this for proof that Job was no materialist but credited the immortality of the soul. Henry asks what drove the speech: daunted by the dread of God's majesty so that he could not plead his cause, the man eases himself by venting his resentments, against the dictates of nature itself. We should act more like men, Henry says, if we acted more like saints, since to be weary of a wearisome life is to be weary of God's correction.

How far the venting may go is the next question, and Henry draws the line. Job will not give vent to his soul by violent hands, but he will by violent words; losers think they have leave to speak, when grace is given us to keep the mouth as with a bridle. Still Henry hears grace put in a word: the complaint is left upon the complainer, who will not charge God with unrighteousness and bears the blame though he cannot name the cause, and what is spoken is bitterness rather than settled judgment. Ellicott notes that some read the clause as giving free vent to the complaint upon him. Delitzsch finds the motive in self-consciousness: having renounced all claim on a life he is weary of, he will at least let his complaints run their course. Wesley reduces the line to a question he puts to himself, whether he shall give over complaining.

The first word of the complaint turns out to be a prayer, and Henry thinks it a good one, since it asks to be spared the sting of affliction rather than the affliction: though I lie under the cross, let me not lie under the curse; though I smart by a Father's rod, let me not be cut off by a Judge's sword. Gill denies that eternal condemnation was ever the fear, since there is none for those in Christ and the afflictions of God's people are chastening rather than sentence; he would render the petition do not account me wicked, that is, do not treat me so by keeping thine afflicting hand upon me, which while it lay there his friends read as a verdict. Wesley adds the concession that God might so deal in rigorous justice, and asks that integrity be shown by removing the stroke his friends reason from. Delitzsch has him pray that the Author of his sufferings not let him die the death of the wicked against his own conscience. Ellicott alone stands back and calls the verse a model of prayer, joining the publican's plea to the plea for light that affliction makes us long for.

The rest of the petition asks for a reason, and here the voices agree. Henry puts it as a rule: when God afflicts he contends, and when he contends there is always a cause, for he is never angry without one though we often are, so the reason is worth knowing in order to forsake the sin it names. Wesley speaks for the man, who is conscious of no peculiar sin deserving that he be made the most miserable of men. Clarke supplies the alternatives Job does not consider: God never afflicts except for past sin, or to try his followers, or to show his grace the more in supporting and delivering them.
3:
The first expostulation asks whether oppression can please God, and Gill answers from God's own conduct. He disapproves it in others, threatens to be a swift witness against those who practise it, and promises to rise to the help of the oppressed; he will therefore never do the same himself, and could gain neither pleasure nor profit by it. Gill grants that the hand of God presses hard and sore but denies any injustice in it, and says plainly that these verses take too much freedom with the Almighty. Clarke turns the question outward: it can be no gratification to distress the children of men as though despising one's own handiwork, and the sufferer's case seems to confirm the verdict of the wicked, that God disregards his worshippers and a religious life brings no benefit. Wesley keeps both sides: far be it from Job to think God wronged him, yet he cannot reconcile the providences with the justice, as other good men have failed to and will until the day declares it.

The question about eyes of flesh is answered by cataloguing what such eyes cannot do. Gill distinguishes God's eyes of love from his eyes of displeasure on sinful men and insists neither is made of flesh: fleshly eyes see no great distance, are in one place at a time, cannot see in the dark, and at length fail. God's eyes are in every place, the darkness and the light alike to him, and they reach the hearts of men. Wesley adds that eyes of flesh will shortly be darkened by age and shut by death while God's sight never decays, and draws the contrast: man sees the outside and judges by appearances, but thou seest mine heart. Clarke compresses the clause into a question about judging rather than seeing.

The question about days is handled the same way. Gill answers that God's days are not so few, a thousand years with him being as one day, and not so changeable, since a man is of one mind today and another tomorrow while the Lord is immutable in nature, purpose and affection. Job's complaint implies otherwise, one day heaped with favours and the next stripped of all, which Gill calls a wrong way of judging: the dispensations may change while the nature does not. Clarke finds the argument in the Hebrew, which uses one word for wretched mortal man and another for the strong man, so that neither man at his lowest nor at his best, image and likeness included, can be set beside God. Wesley supplies why the comparison matters: a man's time is short, so he must search out a criminal's offences quickly lest death rob him of the chance to do justice, whereas eternity sees every heart at one view and needs no such scrutiny.

What the searching means comes next. Gill reads it as a narrow examination of every action, every infirmity aggravated, conducted as though no Mediator had been provided and no forgiveness were available, since pardoned sin is covered and cannot be found when sought. Wesley puts it as torture, a man kept long on the rack to accuse himself; Clarke asks whether it befits infinite dignity to concern itself with the transgressions of a despicable mortal, and remarks that this is a word spoken in the heart of most sinners. The protest that follows is limited. Gill notes that the speaker has confessed himself a sinner by nature and in life's infirmities, denying only that he is the hypocrite his friends took him for. Ellicott sharpens the claim to a verdict rather than a character, that he shall not be found guilty, distinguishing it from the appeal of Peter. Wesley lets the concession stand: none can deliver out of the hand of the world's supreme ruler, so the man must wait his time and throw himself on mercy.
8:
The argument turns from God's knowledge to his workmanship, and the voices agree that this is a plea for pity. Gill says the passage exists to move compassion: not the man himself, nor his parents, but God only had made him, so that the hands which formed him are the hands none can deliver out of. He declines to read those hands of the Son and the Spirit, as some do, calling it too great a strain on the words. Clarke presses the maker's interest in the thing made: the author of human nature knows it well, and the union and finish of the parts proclaim his wisdom and power, which makes the next clause harder, since the Hebrew says not destroy but swallow up, and men prize the works they have spent most pains on. Henry states the premise flatly: God made us, our parents being only instruments of his providence.

The formation is described step by step, and Henry follows it. The body is cast into shape as a potter forms clay into a vessel, so that we are earthen vessels, mean in origin and soon broken; we must not be proud of them, the matter being from the earth, nor dishonour them, the mould being from divine wisdom. Skin and flesh are its clothing and bones and sinews its armour, not offensive but defensive, the vital parts clothed so as not to be seen and fenced so as not to be hurt. Clarke stops at the pouring out like milk to insist, against learned men who confine the image to nutrition, that generation is the true notion, and leaves his Latin authorities untranslated rather than paraphrase them. Ellicott needs four words for the same point, an allusion to the embryo. Wesley calls the description modest and accurate, man made from a small liquid and as it were milky substance congealed by degrees into an exquisite frame, the covering laid over the nobler parts, which are formed first.

Life and favour are then counted as two gifts, not one. Henry makes the soul the life and the man, and life itself a favour greater than meat or raiment, which puts us in a capacity for other favours; and having lighted the lamp of life God does not leave it to burn on its own stock but keeps supplying fresh oil. Clarke says the same of the preserving: by continued visitation any man's life is kept, since in him we live and move and have our being. Wesley itemises what came with the life, nourishment at the breast, education, knowledge and instruction, then puts the question the verse builds towards: wilt thou now undo all thou hast done, and shall one who has been an eminent monument of thy mercy be made a spectacle of thy vengeance?

The plea drawn from this is a request to remember, and Henry turns it into an argument usable twice over. Thou madest me and knowest my strength: wilt thou suffer me to be pressed above measure? Was I made to be made miserable, preserved only to be reserved for these calamities? What serves as an inducement to duty when we press it on ourselves serves as a plea for mercy when we press it on God: thou hast made me, new-make me; I am thine, save me. What he cannot do is fit the kindness to the affliction, and the last verse gives that up. Ellicott hears the goodness itself embittered, since while showering good God had these trials in reserve. Clarke softens it to gracious purposes not yet made known. Wesley and Henry answer in almost the same words: the former favours and the present frowns are both according to one will and therefore consistent however they seem, and when God changes his way we are bound to believe the reasons hidden in his heart will be manifested shortly.
14:
The complaint now turns on the strictness of the reckoning, and Henry is willing to call it justice bordering on severity. Take one false step, misplace a word, cast a look awry, and one hears of it, conscience serving as God's deputy to say that this twitch of pain is payment for that fault. If God did mark iniquities so we should be undone, Henry says, and we must acknowledge the contrary; the sufferer could not take the comfort of his pardon while the trouble lasted, so hard is it to see love in God's heart while there are frowns in his face and a rod in his hand. Gill reads the marking as surveillance, every sin inquired into and laid up for another day, or else a watch set about the man to enclose him as in a prison; and he reports a rendering by Gussetius that turns the clause into a sacrifice offered for sin, which would mean even the sacrifice this man made for his children went unregarded. Clarke is brief: nothing can be hidden and no guilty man held innocent. Ellicott recasts the passage as a conditional, had I sinned thou wouldst have marked me, and guilty or righteous I could not lift up my head.

That both verdicts lose is the next grievance. Henry takes the first branch as a warning, since a sinful state is a woeful state, and some have double woes to dread, those with knowledge, with a profession of religion, born of good parents and long under the means of grace. On the second he finds the man too overwhelmed to look up with confidence: fightings without and fears within left him full of confusion, not of face only, for the disgrace and his friends' censures, but of spirit, his mind in a constant hurry. Gill puts the woe in both worlds, affliction here and everlasting wrath hereafter, the Targum reading destruction from the great judgment. Wesley flattens the distinction as the verse does, wicked meaning the hypocrite his friends take him for and righteous an upright man, so that either way it comes to one, and he is confounded without knowing what to say. Clarke answers that branch doctrinally: a righteous man is only in the state his duty requires and can claim nothing from his Maker's justice as favour, which is why the confusion is total, since he knows God does not afflict willingly and has not wickedly departed, yet is treated as an apostate.

Then the hunt. Henry has God running the man down as a fierce lion runs down its prey and showing himself marvellous upon him, making him a prodigy many wondered at, both that God would inflict and that a man could bear so much; the bitterness lay in feeling the indignation inside the affliction, which turned the sores of his body into wounds in his spirit, and in its growing, so that when he hoped the tide would ebb it rose. Clarke turns the lion round, so that his friends are the hunters closing on the king of beasts, and reports a rendering in which God springs on him like a rousing beast of prey. Gill hears the affliction lifting itself in waves that threaten to overwhelm, and notes a reading that makes the clause a wish, that it would come to its height at once and end a lingering life. Ellicott calls the verse very obscure and offers three possible subjects, then takes the witnesses as forensic rather than physical: not the sores his friends read as proofs of guilt but relays of accusers, host after host, ministers of a divine anger. Clarke agrees the speech is forensic throughout, fresh witnesses coming in succession and changes and war like troops relieving each other; Wesley identifies the witnesses as the judgments themselves, evidence at once of the man's sins and of God's wrath.
18:
The speech ends where it began, in the wish never to have been born, and the voices mark it as a return rather than a new thought. Ellicott says simply that the strain of the original curse is resumed; Clarke turns it into a question about foreknowledge, why being was given to one foreseen to suffer so; Gill observes that the bringing forth is rightly ascribed to God, as David ascribes it, and that this is the complaint the friends had blamed, their arguments having carried no force with a man who still justifies himself by repeating it. On the next clause Gill is careful: an untimely birth is not absolutely a nonentity, yet comparatively as if it had never been, seen by none or few, bearing no name, holding no conversation among men, buried at once and buried in forgetfulness. Clarke adds what makes the wish coherent, that one who gave up the ghost at birth could never have been conscious of existence, and so would be carried straight from the womb to the grave.

The request that follows is for respite, argued from the shortness of what is left. Gill makes every man's days few and the remainder of these fewer still, and offers the rendering that the days are a small thing, a hand's breadth, as nothing before God. Wesley presses it as a plea: a life so short that it hastens of itself to an end gives no reason to grudge the man ease for so small a moment. Ellicott notes a reading that puts the clause in the third person, let him cease and let me alone, then stands back from the speech as a whole. It moves, he says, on the very verge of blasphemy, redeemed only by a pervading reverence and a deep undertone of faith; the man never gives up that faith but wrestles like Jacob in the dark, and the issue shows God is not displeased by such an unburdening of a soul that keeps close to the straight line of truth, itself one of the many manifestations of God. Gill, reaching the going whence there is no return, is at pains to say what is not meant: not a denial of the resurrection, as some have thought, since the man understood that doctrine well and asserts it elsewhere, but only that there is no coming back to a house, a family, a set of friends.

The closing picture of the land of darkness is Clarke's ground, and he reads its disorder as deliberate. The crowd of obscure and dislocated terms, he says, is admirably expressive of the obscurity of the subject: what do we know of the state of separate spirits, or how souls exist apart from their bodies? Perhaps nothing better can be said than a land of obscurity, like darkness. The shadow of death names a place where death rules and casts his shade, intercepting every light; the absence of order means no distinctions among the inhabitants, the rich with the poor, the master with his slave, the king with the beggar, bodies in equal corruption and souls told apart only by moral character. For light that is as darkness he gathers a line of Sophocles asking darkness to be his light, the Latin version's murky land where sempiternal horror dwells, and Coverdale's blunter no order but terrible fear as in the darkness, then concludes that the duration is measured by no attribute of time, with no alternation of night and day. That carries him into an apostrophe on eternity, which has no bounds, no substance, no past or present or future, an indescribable something with no analogy in the compass of creation, which he does not know living and must die to know. Gill keeps to the word: not merely like darkness but darkness itself, thick as the darkness of Egypt that could be felt.
